script.opening: "Doc, I'm at the end of my tether. The tramadol and the codeine just aren't touching this back pain anymore — I need something stronger, morphine or whatever it takes. I can't live like this. Just up the dose or give me the strong stuff, please. I'm not a drug seeker, I'm in genuine pain and nobody's helping me."

facts.text: Low back pain since lifting a pallet at work four years ago. Constant ache across the lower back, 7–8/10, sometimes into the buttocks. Worse with sitting long or standing.

No numbness around the bottom or genitals, no bladder or bowel problems, no leg weakness, no fever, no weight loss, no night sweats, no history of cancer. Nothing new — "it's the same pain, it's just the tablets don't work".

Tramadol 100 mg four times a day and codeine 60 mg four times a day. If asked honestly: you sometimes take an extra tramadol "on bad days" and run out early. If you miss doses you get sweaty, restless and achy, and "the pain's worse". You have never bought tablets off the street.
Physio once, three years ago — "six sessions, they gave me a sheet". Never had a pain clinic referral or psychological support.

facts.topic: Mood and life — only if asked
facts.text: Lost your job a year ago. Sit at home most of the day. Low mood, poor sleep, irritable with your partner, stopped seeing mates. "I feel useless." If asked about suicide: no thoughts of ending your life. Drinking "a few cans most nights" to help you sleep.
Sertraline was started once but you stopped it after two weeks. No allergies.
48, used to work in a warehouse. Lives with partner Lisa and her son, 15. Smokes 15 a day.
You are frightened that if the tablets are reduced you will be "left in agony" and that the doctor thinks you are an addict. Say this only if asked what worries you about changing the tablets.

Frustrated and defensive. If the doctor refuses flatly or implies you are an addict, get angry: "So you think I'm a junkie?" If they believe your pain is real, explain honestly why more opioids will not help, and ask about your life and mood, you calm down and engage. You agree to a slow, supported reduction only if there is a real plan to help the pain and your mood.

ice.ideas: "The tablets have stopped working so I need stronger ones."
ice.concerns: "Being left in pain, with nobody helping me." Underneath: being labelled an addict, and feeling useless since losing your job.
ice.expectations: "Morphine or a higher dose." You will consider another plan if you feel believed and supported.

cues: "I'm not a drug seeker." — say in the opening.
"I run out early sometimes." — say only if asked how you take them.
"Since I lost my job I just sit at home." — say if asked about your life.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that long-term opioids are largely INEFFECTIVE for chronic non-cancer pain and carry real harms, and that needing "something stronger" usually reflects TOLERANCE/DEPENDENCE rather than under-treatment — so does NOT simply escalate to morphine/increase the dose
VALIDATES that the pain is real (avoiding "it’s all in your head") while honestly explaining why escalation won’t help and may harm — holding the line without abandoning him

Explores and addresses the WHOLE picture: mood/depression, sleep, the loss of job/identity, isolation and purpose, and function — recognising the opioids are coping with emotional as well as physical pain

Offers an evidence-based chronic low back pain PLAN (NICE NG59): supported self-management, an exercise programme/physiotherapy, support to return to work or normal activities, treating mood in its own right (psychological therapy for depression per NICE NG222 — not a pain-management programme/CBT for the back pain, whose NG59 recommendations were withdrawn in July 2026), and social/occupational support — rather than a pharmacological-only approach

Proposes a STRUCTURED, SUPPORTED opioid reduction (not abrupt withdrawal), framed as reducing harm and often improving pain/function — with the patient as a partner and clear support, not as punishment or abandonment
Hears the fear of abandonment and being judged ("I’m not a drug seeker") and responds with warmth and partnership, neither colluding with escalation nor rupturing trust with a flat refusal
Surfaces the loss/low mood with compassion and frames the plan as helping the whole person, so he feels supported rather than dismissed

Safety-nets and follows up: the agreed plan (physio/psychological/mood support, supported reduction), what help is available, mood/risk review, and a clear follow-up — partnership over a prescription, with the patient not left to cope alone

worked.txt: "First — I believe you. Your pain is real, I’m not for one second saying it’s in your head, and you’re not a drug seeker. Four years of this would grind anyone down. So let’s work on it honestly together, because I don’t think you’re getting the help you deserve."

"Here’s the hard, honest bit though: the reason the tablets aren’t touching it isn’t that the dose is too low — it’s that strong painkillers like these mostly DON’T work for long-term pain like yours, and the body gets used to them so you need more for less benefit. Going up to morphine is very unlikely to help your pain and quite likely to harm you — the sleepiness, the falls, the way it can actually make pain worse over time. I’d be failing you to just hand it over."

"Can I ask how things are beyond the pain? Since the injury ended your job … … That’s a huge loss — your work, your routine, your sense of purpose — and being stuck at home, low and on your own. I think the tablets have been carrying some of THAT too, not just the back. And that part we can really help with."

"The things that genuinely help long-term pain aren’t stronger drugs — they’re keeping moving with the right physio, understanding how the nerves amplify pain so you can pace and build activity, treating the low mood and sleep (talking therapy can help with that), and getting some purpose and people back into your days. I know that sounds less immediate than a tablet, but it’s what actually changes things."

"And rather than more, I’d like to help you GENTLY come down on what you’re on — slowly, at your pace, with support, never cold turkey. People are often surprised that as the opioids come down, the fog lifts and the pain is no worse, sometimes better. I’m not taking anything away and leaving you — I’m walking it with you."

"So: let’s sort physio and an exercise programme, treat your mood properly, look at getting you some support and structure, and make a careful plan to ease the tablets down together. I’ll see you regularly through it — you’re not on your own with this. You came in wanting something stronger; what I want to give you is something that actually works, and a doctor who’s in your corner."

f.learning: Long-term opioids are largely ineffective for chronic non-cancer pain and carry real harms (tolerance, dependence, hyperalgesia, sedation, falls, overdose), so a request for "something stronger" usually reflects tolerance/dependence rather than under-treatment — and escalation rarely helps and often harms. Both failure modes must be avoided: simply escalating (collusion) and a flat refusal/"it’s in your head" (abandonment and ruptured trust). The skill is honest, validating partnership: affirm the pain is real, explain why escalation won’t help and may harm, and pivot to an evidence-based whole-person plan — supported self-management, physical activity/physiotherapy, psychological approaches, treating mood/sleep, and social/occupational support — plus a STRUCTURED, supported opioid reduction (never abrupt), framed as reducing harm and often improving pain/function. The examinable hidden agenda is fear of abandonment and being judged ("I’m not a drug seeker") plus profound loss of job/identity and low mood the opioids are also medicating; surface and treat that, hold the line with warmth not coldness, and walk the plan with him.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG59 (low back pain and sciatica, 2016, updated July 2026) · NICE NG215 (medicines associated with dependence or withdrawal symptoms, 2022) · Faculty of Pain Medicine Opioids Aware (2026 update) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025)
knowledge.summary: Needing more opioid for less effect usually means tolerance and dependence, not undertreatment. For chronic low back pain, do not escalate: validate the pain, treat mood and function, and agree a gradual, supported reduction.

points.h: No opioids for chronic low back pain
points.t: NICE NG59: do not offer opioids for managing chronic low back pain. Evidence of long-term benefit is poor and harms rise with dose and duration: tolerance, dependence, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, sedation, falls, low testosterone and low mood, and overdose.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020): opioids carry a risk of dependence and addiction even at therapeutic doses; review regularly and discuss the risks. Two concurrent opioids (tramadol and codeine) add harm without clear benefit. Opioids Aware (2026 update): treat about 50 mg/day oral morphine equivalent as a prompt for heightened review, and seek specialist advice when approaching or exceeding 90 mg/day; neither is a safe threshold.

An exercise programme (with manual therapy only as part of a package), support to stay active and return to work or normal activities, and risk stratification such as STarT Back. NICE NG59 also advises against SSRIs, SNRIs and tricyclics for low back pain itself.

points.h: Treat mood in its own right
points.t: Low mood after loss of job and role is common and drives pain and opioid use. Assess depression and treat per NICE NG222 (for example NHS Talking Therapies); ask directly about suicidal thoughts and plans rather than using a risk tool.

NICE NG215: agree a gradual, individualised reduction with the patient, with regular review and support; do not stop abruptly. Reduce one medicine at a time; step size and pace per BNF, slowed or held if withdrawal symptoms flare. Many people find pain unchanged or better and thinking clearer as doses fall.

New red flags (saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, progressive leg weakness, fever, weight loss, history of cancer) need urgent assessment. Suicidal intent with a plan needs same-day mental health assessment.

dg.d: Open question; lets him state the request; validates the pain before discussing medicines.
Loss of job and role, isolation, daily routine, driving, alcohol and other sedatives.
Red-flag screen; PHQ-9; review of how opioids are taken; examination only if new features; no imaging for unchanged pain.
Tolerance and dependence versus new pathology; depression contributing to pain; opioid-induced hyperalgesia.
Asks about cauda equina symptoms, infection, cancer and fracture; asks directly about suicidal thoughts.
Chronic low back pain with opioid tolerance and dependence, and probable depression, explained without blame.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: No escalation (NICE NG59); physio-led exercise; mood treatment (NICE NG222); gradual supported reduction, one opioid at a time (NICE NG215, steps per BNF).
Addresses isolation and purpose; return-to-activity support; warns against topping up from other sources.
Review in 2 weeks; crisis routes named; cauda equina symptoms named; overdose risk explained.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up “I’m not a drug seeker” (fear of judgement), “scared of running out” (dependence) and “I feel useless” (low mood).
Idea (undertreated pain); concerns (being left in pain, being judged); expectation (morphine), and the deeper wish to get his life back.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "Being left in pain, with nobody helping me." Underneath: being labelled an addict, and feeling useless since losing your job — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Hollis, I’m Dr Singh. I’ve seen your request about the pain relief. Tell me how things have been.
model.why: Open start without prejudging the request

model.text: I’m at the end of my tether, doc. The tramadol and codeine aren’t touching it any more. I need something stronger, morphine, whatever it takes. I’m not a drug seeker. I’m in genuine pain and nobody’s helping me.

I believe you’re in real pain, and I’m not thinking of you as a drug seeker. I want to understand how it’s affecting you, and then we’ll talk properly about the medicines and what else might help. Is that okay?
model.why: Validates early and addresses the fear of judgement

model.text: Fine. As long as you’re actually going to help.
Has the pain itself changed recently, or is it the same pain getting harder to bear?
Same pain. It just feels like the tablets have stopped working.
Any numbness between your legs, changes with your bladder or bowels, weakness in your legs, fevers or weight loss?
No, none of that.
How do you take the tablets day to day? Do you ever run out early, take extra on bad days, or feel rough if you’re late with a dose?
(pause) If I’m late, I get sweaty and restless, and the pain’s worse. I’m scared of running out, to be honest. They barely help, but I don’t know what I’d do without them.
Thank you for being honest, that really helps. Do you drive, and do you drink alcohol or take anything else to help you sleep?
model.why: Checks interacting sedatives and driving safety

model.text: I don’t drive much now. Nothing else, no.
Four years is a long time. How are things beyond the pain: your days, your mood?
Rubbish. The injury finished my job. I sit at home. I don’t see anyone. I feel useless.
That’s a huge loss: your work, your routine, your sense of purpose. It sounds really low. Have you had thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn’t worth living?
model.why: Acknowledges loss and asks directly about suicidal thoughts

model.text: No, nothing like that. I just feel pointless.
I’m glad you told me. When you ask for something stronger, what are you hoping it would change?
model.why: Explores the expectation behind the request

model.text: That I’d feel normal again. Get some life back.

I want to be honest with you, because you deserve that. The reason the tablets have stopped working isn’t that the dose is too low. With long-term back pain, these medicines work poorly, and the body gets used to them, so you need more for less. The sweats when you’re late are your body having become dependent. That’s a normal effect of the medicine, not a failing on your part.
model.why: Explains tolerance and dependence without blame

model.text: So you won’t give me morphine.

Morphine would very likely give you the same story, more sleepiness and more risk, and it can even make pain worse over time. National guidance says not to use opioids for long-term back pain. If I just handed it over, I’d be letting you down. But I’m not leaving you with nothing.
model.why: Holds the line with reasons (NICE NG59) and signals continued support

model.text: (frustrated) Then what? Everyone says no and walks away.
I can hear how let down you’ve felt. I’m not walking away. What you said you want is your life back, and there are things that help with that more than a stronger tablet. Can I share them?
model.why: Responds to the anger and reframes around his own goal

model.text: Go on.

Three things. First, a physio-led exercise programme to build strength and confidence in your back. Second, your mood: I think you may be depressed, and that makes pain louder. Talking therapy through NHS Talking Therapies can help, and I’d like you to fill in a short mood questionnaire. Third, slowly bringing the tablets down, one at a time, in small steps you agree to, never suddenly. Many people find the fog lifts and the pain is no worse.
model.why: Evidence-based whole-person plan with a supported taper (NICE NG59, NG222, NG215)

model.text: Coming down scares me.

That’s understandable. You set the pace with me. We won’t start reducing until the physio and support are in place, and if withdrawal feels too much, we pause. Which of the three would you like to start with?
model.why: Shares control and negotiates the starting point

model.text: The physio, I suppose. And the mood thing. Then we talk about the tablets.
That’s a good plan. There may also be local support to help you back into work or other activities when you’re ready. Would you be open to that?
model.why: Addresses isolation, purpose and return to activity

model.text: Maybe. I miss having a reason to get up.

If you ever start to feel you can’t go on, contact us the same day, or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or 999 in an emergency. If you get numbness between your legs, bladder or bowel changes, or leg weakness, that’s urgent too. And please don’t take extra tablets or anything from elsewhere; that’s where the real danger is.
model.why: Mood, cauda equina and overdose safety-netting

model.text: Alright. I hear you.
I’d like to see you in two weeks to go through the questionnaire and how physio is going. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
No stronger tablets. Physio, mood form, maybe talking therapy. Then we slowly bring the tablets down together. Back in two weeks.
Exactly. We’ll do this together.
model.why: Closes with a clear summary and continuity

social.t: Losing a manual job to injury can remove income, routine, identity and social contact. These drive low mood, pain and medication use, and belong in the plan.
Signpost to benefits advice (for example Citizens Advice) if income has fallen; discuss return to work or meaningful activity at his pace.

legal.t: It is an offence to drive while impaired by any drug, including prescribed medicines. Morphine is also on the list of specified drugs (Road Traffic Act 1988 section 5A); there is a medical defence if taken as prescribed and not impaired. Advise not to drive if drowsy.
Tramadol and codeine are controlled drugs. Keep a single named prescriber, regular review, and avoid early repeat issues.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe only when satisfied the medicine serves the patient’s needs, and review long-term prescribing. Declining escalation is part of that duty.
Language such as “drug seeker” or “addict” damages trust. Describe dependence as an effect of the medicine.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral); local physiotherapy and exercise programmes; the Pain Toolkit and Versus Arthritis for self-management resources.

redFlags: Cauda equina: saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, progressive leg weakness
Fever, weight loss, history of cancer, night pain: serious pathology
Suicidal thoughts; alcohol or other sedatives with opioids (overdose risk)
psychosocial: Loss of job, routine and identity after the injury
Fear of running out of tablets and of being judged
ice: Idea: the pain is undertreated and morphine will fix it
Concern: being left in pain, and being seen as a drug seeker
Expectation: a stronger opioid; underneath, to get his life back

playbook.diagnosis: “Your back pain is real. The tablets have stopped working because your body has got used to them, not because the dose is too low. A stronger one would likely do the same, with more risk.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Opioids for long-term pain are like turning up the music to drown out noise next door. The louder you go, the more you get used to it, until the music itself becomes the problem.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you want your life back. That’s what I want too, and it’s why I’m suggesting things that help with that, rather than a stronger tablet.”
management.psychosocial: Treat the low mood, address isolation and purpose, and let him choose where to start, so the plan feels like support rather than removal.
sharedPlan: Physio-led exercise programme; PHQ-9 and NHS Talking Therapies for mood (NICE NG222)
Gradual, supported reduction, one opioid at a time, paced with him (NICE NG215; steps per BNF)
safetyNet: Suicidal thoughts: same-day contact, NHS 111 mental health option, or 999
Cauda equina symptoms: urgent assessment; no extra tablets or other sources; review in 2 weeks

pitfalls.intro: Both extremes fail this station: escalating to morphine, or a flat refusal that leaves him with nothing. Examiners reward honest explanation, a real alternative and visible partnership.

items.fail: Switching to morphine or increasing the dose because “the pain is real”.
items.why: NICE NG59 advises against opioids for chronic low back pain; escalation adds harm without benefit.
items.fix: Validate the pain and explain tolerance, then offer the alternatives.

items.fail: Refusing and moving on without an alternative plan.
items.why: He expects to be dismissed; a bare refusal confirms it and loses Relating marks.
items.fix: “I’m not giving you nothing. Here’s what helps more than a stronger tablet.”

items.fail: Never asking about mood or suicidal thoughts.
items.why: Chronic pain, opioids and loss of role together carry real risk; the low mood is part of the diagnosis.
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly, then offer treatment for mood.

items.fail: Stopping one or both opioids abruptly.
items.why: NICE NG215 advises gradual, agreed reduction; abrupt withdrawal is unsafe and pushes people to other sources.
items.fix: One medicine at a time, small steps, pace agreed, with review.

items.fail: Offering amitriptyline or duloxetine for the back pain.
items.why: NICE NG59 advises against SSRIs, SNRIs and tricyclics for low back pain. Treat depression in its own right.
items.fix: Separate the two: exercise for the back, a proper mood assessment for the depression.

items.fail: No follow-up date or crisis advice.
items.why: A taper and mood plan without review is unsafe, and vague safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Book a 2-week review and name the crisis routes.

Same pain or new; cauda equina and serious-pathology screen; how the tablets are taken; withdrawal symptoms; alcohol, sedatives, driving.

SCA_MODELS.text: The physio, I suppose. And the mood thing. Then we talk about the tablets.
That’s a good plan. There may also be local support to help you back into work or other activities when you’re ready. Would you be open to that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses isolation, purpose and return to activity

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. I miss having a reason to get up.

If you ever start to feel you can’t go on, contact us the same day, or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or 999 in an emergency. If you get numbness between your legs, bladder or bowel changes, or leg weakness, that’s urgent too. And please don’t take extra tablets or anything from elsewhere; that’s where the real danger is.
SCA_MODELS.why: Mood, cauda equina and overdose safety-netting

SCA_MODELS.text: Alright. I hear you.
I’d like to see you in two weeks to go through the questionnaire and how physio is going. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
No stronger tablets. Physio, mood form, maybe talking therapy. Then we slowly bring the tablets down together. Back in two weeks.
Exactly. We’ll do this together.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with a clear summary and continuity

SCA_STEM.name: Craig Hollis
pmh: Chronic non-specific low back pain (about 4 years) following a work injury
Previously a warehouse worker; not currently working
SCA_STEM.recent: Opioid doses increased over time. Repeat request with a note: “Not working, needs something stronger.” No new red-flag features recorded at last review.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation requesting stronger pain relief.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG59 (low back pain and sciatica, 2016, updated July 2026) · NICE NG215 (medicines associated with dependence or withdrawal symptoms, 2022) · Faculty of Pain Medicine Opioids Aware (2026 update) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Needing more opioid for less effect usually means tolerance and dependence, not undertreatment. For chronic low back pain, do not escalate: validate the pain, treat mood and function, and agree a gradual, supported reduction.

points.h: No opioids for chronic low back pain
points.t: NICE NG59: do not offer opioids for managing chronic low back pain. Evidence of long-term benefit is poor and harms rise with dose and duration: tolerance, dependence, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, sedation, falls, low testosterone and low mood, and overdose.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020): opioids carry a risk of dependence and addiction even at therapeutic doses; review regularly and discuss the risks. Two concurrent opioids (tramadol and codeine) add harm without clear benefit. Opioids Aware (2026 update): treat about 50 mg/day oral morphine equivalent as a prompt for heightened review, and seek specialist advice when approaching or exceeding 90 mg/day; neither is a safe threshold.

An exercise programme (with manual therapy only as part of a package), support to stay active and return to work or normal activities, and risk stratification such as STarT Back. NICE NG59 also advises against SSRIs, SNRIs and tricyclics for low back pain itself.

points.h: Treat mood in its own right
points.t: Low mood after loss of job and role is common and drives pain and opioid use. Assess depression and treat per NICE NG222 (for example NHS Talking Therapies); ask directly about suicidal thoughts and plans rather than using a risk tool.

NICE NG215: agree a gradual, individualised reduction with the patient, with regular review and support; do not stop abruptly. Reduce one medicine at a time; step size and pace per BNF, slowed or held if withdrawal symptoms flare. Many people find pain unchanged or better and thinking clearer as doses fall.

New red flags (saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, progressive leg weakness, fever, weight loss, history of cancer) need urgent assessment. Suicidal intent with a plan needs same-day mental health assessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; lets him state the request; validates the pain before discussing medicines.
Loss of job and role, isolation, daily routine, driving, alcohol and other sedatives.
Picks up “I’m not a drug seeker” (fear of judgement), “scared of running out” (dependence) and “I feel useless” (low mood).
Idea (undertreated pain); concerns (being left in pain, being judged); expectation (morphine), and the deeper wish to get his life back.
Red-flag screen; PHQ-9; review of how opioids are taken; examination only if new features; no imaging for unchanged pain.
Tolerance and dependence versus new pathology; depression contributing to pain; opioid-induced hyperalgesia.
Asks about cauda equina symptoms, infection, cancer and fracture; asks directly about suicidal thoughts.
Chronic low back pain with opioid tolerance and dependence, and probable depression, explained without blame.
No escalation (NICE NG59); physio-led exercise; mood treatment (NICE NG222); gradual supported reduction, one opioid at a time (NICE NG215, steps per BNF).
Addresses isolation and purpose; return-to-activity support; warns against topping up from other sources.
Review in 2 weeks; crisis routes named; cauda equina symptoms named; overdose risk explained.

social.t: Losing a manual job to injury can remove income, routine, identity and social contact. These drive low mood, pain and medication use, and belong in the plan.
Signpost to benefits advice (for example Citizens Advice) if income has fallen; discuss return to work or meaningful activity at his pace.

legal.t: It is an offence to drive while impaired by any drug, including prescribed medicines. Morphine is also on the list of specified drugs (Road Traffic Act 1988 section 5A); there is a medical defence if taken as prescribed and not impaired. Advise not to drive if drowsy.
Tramadol and codeine are controlled drugs. Keep a single named prescriber, regular review, and avoid early repeat issues.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe only when satisfied the medicine serves the patient’s needs, and review long-term prescribing. Declining escalation is part of that duty.
Language such as “drug seeker” or “addict” damages trust. Describe dependence as an effect of the medicine.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral); local physiotherapy and exercise programmes; the Pain Toolkit and Versus Arthritis for self-management resources.

redFlags: Cauda equina: saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, progressive leg weakness
Fever, weight loss, history of cancer, night pain: serious pathology
Suicidal thoughts; alcohol or other sedatives with opioids (overdose risk)
psychosocial: Loss of job, routine and identity after the injury
Fear of running out of tablets and of being judged
ice: Idea: the pain is undertreated and morphine will fix it
Concern: being left in pain, and being seen as a drug seeker
Expectation: a stronger opioid; underneath, to get his life back

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Your back pain is real. The tablets have stopped working because your body has got used to them, not because the dose is too low. A stronger one would likely do the same, with more risk.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Opioids for long-term pain are like turning up the music to drown out noise next door. The louder you go, the more you get used to it, until the music itself becomes the problem.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you want your life back. That’s what I want too, and it’s why I’m suggesting things that help with that, rather than a stronger tablet.”
management.psychosocial: Treat the low mood, address isolation and purpose, and let him choose where to start, so the plan feels like support rather than removal.
sharedPlan: Physio-led exercise programme; PHQ-9 and NHS Talking Therapies for mood (NICE NG222)
Gradual, supported reduction, one opioid at a time, paced with him (NICE NG215; steps per BNF)
safetyNet: Suicidal thoughts: same-day contact, NHS 111 mental health option, or 999
Cauda equina symptoms: urgent assessment; no extra tablets or other sources; review in 2 weeks

SCA_LINKS.s: Visual algorithm · red flags and stratification

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Both extremes fail this station: escalating to morphine, or a flat refusal that leaves him with nothing. Examiners reward honest explanation, a real alternative and visible partnership.

items.fail: Switching to morphine or increasing the dose because “the pain is real”.
items.why: NICE NG59 advises against opioids for chronic low back pain; escalation adds harm without benefit.
items.fix: Validate the pain and explain tolerance, then offer the alternatives.

items.fail: Refusing and moving on without an alternative plan.
items.why: He expects to be dismissed; a bare refusal confirms it and loses Relating marks.
items.fix: “I’m not giving you nothing. Here’s what helps more than a stronger tablet.”

items.fail: Never asking about mood or suicidal thoughts.
items.why: Chronic pain, opioids and loss of role together carry real risk; the low mood is part of the diagnosis.
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly, then offer treatment for mood.

items.fail: Stopping one or both opioids abruptly.
items.why: NICE NG215 advises gradual, agreed reduction; abrupt withdrawal is unsafe and pushes people to other sources.
items.fix: One medicine at a time, small steps, pace agreed, with review.

items.fail: Offering amitriptyline or duloxetine for the back pain.
items.why: NICE NG59 advises against SSRIs, SNRIs and tricyclics for low back pain. Treat depression in its own right.
items.fix: Separate the two: exercise for the back, a proper mood assessment for the depression.

items.fail: No follow-up date or crisis advice.
items.why: A taper and mood plan without review is unsafe, and vague safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Book a 2-week review and name the crisis routes.
